== History ==
There is a tradition that the shrine was founded during the reign of {{ill|Emperor Jimmu|ar|الإمبراطور جينمو|arz|الامبراطور جينمو|as|জিম্মু|az|Cimmu|bcl|Emperador Jimmu|be|Імператар Дзіму|ca|Jinmu|cdo|Sìng-ū Tiĕng-huòng|ckb|ئیمپراتۆر جینمو|cs|Džimmu|de|Jimmu|el|Αυτοκράτορας Τζίμου|eo|Imperiestro Jinmu|es|Jinmu Tennō|et|Jimmu|eu|Jimmu enperadorea|fa|امپراتور جینمو|fi|Jinmu|fr|Jinmu|hak|Sṳ̀n-vú Thiên-fòng|he|ג'ימו, קיסר יפן|hi|सम्राट जिममु|hr|Jinmu|hu|Dzsinmu japán császár|id|Jimmu|it|Jinmu|ja|神武天皇|jv|Jimmu Tenno|ka|ძიმუ|ko|진무 천황|kw|Emperour Jimmu|la|Jimmu|lt|Imperatorius Džinmu|lv|Džimmu|mn|Эзэн Хаан Жиммү|mr|जिम्मू|ms|Maharaja Jimmu|my|ဂျင်းမူ ဧကရာဇ်|nl|Jimmu|no|Jimmu|pl|Jimmu|pt|Jimmu|ru|Император Дзимму|sh|Car Jimmu|simple|Emperor Jimmu|sl|Cesar Džinmu|sr|Џинму|sv|Jimmu|th|จักรพรรดิจิมมุ|tl|Emperador Jimmu|tr|Jimmu|uk|Імператор Дзімму|uz|Jimmu|vi|Thiên hoàng Jimmu|war|Emperador Jimmu|wuu|神武天皇|zh|神武天皇|zh_classical|神武天皇|zh_min_nan|Sîn-bú Thian-hông|zh_yue|神武天皇|qid=Q200188}}, but this is considered a later attribution, and the precise date and circumstances of its establishment are unknown. In ancient times it was called “Takuzuda Shrine,” without the character for “tama” (soul). The “Takuzuda Shrine” listed among the thirteen shrines of Shimogata District, Tsushima Province, in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|abstract|Q11064932|fr|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|simple|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|zh|延喜式神名帳|qid=Q11064932}} is identified with this shrine. Although the enshrined deities are said to be five deities including Amaterasu Ōmikami, the original deity was {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Takuzuda-no-Kami}}, a god unique to {{ill|Tsushima Island|ar|جزيرة تسوشيما|arz|جزيره تسوشيما|az|Tsuşima|be|Цусіма|bg|Цушима|bn|সুশিমা দ্বীপ|ca|Tsushima (illa)|ceb|Tsushima (kapuloan)|cs|Cušima (Nagasaki)|de|Tsushima (Insel)|el|Νήσος Τσουσίμα|eo|Cuŝima|es|Tsushima (isla)|et|Tsushima|eu|Tsushima (uhartea)|fa|تسوشیما|fi|Tsushima (saaristo)|fj|Tsushima|fr|Tsushima (île)|gl|Tsushima|he|צושימה (אי)|hu|Cusima (Nagaszaki)|hy|Ցուսիմա|id|Pulau Tsushima|it|Tsushima (isola)|ja|対馬|kk|Цусима қаласы|ko|쓰시마섬|ks|ژُشِما لانٛکھ|ky|Цушима|la|Tsusima|lt|Cušima (sala)|ms|Pulau Tsushima|nl|Tsushima (eiland)|no|Tsushima (øygruppe)|pl|Cuszima|pt|Tsushima (ilha)|ro|Insula Tsushima|ru|Цусима|simple|Tsushima Island|sr|Цушима|sv|Tsushima (ögrupp)|sw|Kisiwa cha Tsushima|th|เกาะสึชิมะ|tr|Tsushima Adası|uk|Цусіма (острів)|vi|Tsushima (đảo)|yi|צושימע אינדזל|zh|对马|zh_yue|對馬島|qid=Q52051}}. In the entry for February 5, Jōwa 4 (837) in the 『{{ill|Shoku Nihon Kōki|cs|Šoku Nihonkóki|de|Shoku Nihon Kōki|es|Shoku Nihon Kōki|ff|Shoku Nihon Kōki|fr|Shoku nihon kōki|ja|続日本後紀|ko|속일본후기|pt|Shoku Nihon Kōki|zh|續日本後紀|qid=Q1041301}}』, there is a record of Takuzuto-no-Kami being promoted from no rank to Junior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade, which is thought to refer to the deity of this shrine. The shrine was part of Tsushima’s distinctive syncretic faith known as Tendō worship, which blended Shinto and Buddhism, and functioned together with a Kannon hall, where rituals were conducted by temple priests<ref>{{ill|Masataka Suzuki|ja|鈴木正崇|qid=Q11648975}} “Rituals and Village Space in Tsutsu, Tsushima,” in *Cosmology of Ritual and Space—Tsushima and Okinawa*, Shunjūsha, 2004</ref>. Tendō worship is a syncretism of mother-and-child deity worship, sun worship, mountain worship, and other beliefs. Originally, the shrine had no sanctuary building and instead served as a place of distant worship of the sacred, restricted mountain Tendōyama (Tatera-yama). After the {{ill|Shinbutsu bunri|ca|Shinbutsu bunri|de|Shinbutsu-Bunri|es|Shinbutsu bunri|fa|شینبوتسو بونری|fi|Shinbutsu bunri|fr|Shinbutsu bunri|id|Shinbutsu bunri|it|Shinbutsu bunri|ja|神仏分離|ko|신불분리|ru|Симбуцу бунри|tr|Şinbutsu-bunri|zh|神佛分離|qid=Q1970535}} in the Meiji period, the Kannon hall of Tsutsutera, which had been a shrine temple, was used as the shrine building; however, this Kannon hall was destroyed by fire in 1956<ref>*Nihon Rekishi Chimei Taikei: Nagasaki Prefecture Place Names*, pp. 1011–1012, and *Kadokawa Nihon Chimei Daijiten: Nagasaki Prefecture*, p. 595</ref>.

[[File:Bell of Takuzudama Shrine.jpg|thumb|230px|Temple bell]]
* **Temple bell** — A Japanese-style bell cast in Kōei 3 (1344) by metalworkers from Matsuura in Hizen Province. A long inscription appears in the pond-shaped section above the striking point, stating that the original bell was first made in Kankō 5 (1008) and was recast in Kōei 3 (1344). The craftsmen are identified as the master carpenter Kakuen and the assistant craftsman Suenaka from Yamashita Manor in Kamimatsuura, Hizen Province<ref name="#1"/>.
* **Goryeo-printed Tripitaka** — 3 volumes, 2 fascicles, 1,016 books (with appended *Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* [Japanese edition 318 fascicles, manuscript 6 fascicles], total 324 fascicles), designated in fiscal year 2017<ref>Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology Notification No. 117, September 15, 2017</ref>.

== Theft incident ==
The “{{ill|List of TVB dramas in 2013|ms|Senarai Drama TVB 2013|vi|Danh sách phim TVB năm 2013|zh|翡翠台電視劇集列表 (2013年)|qid=Q82800}}” that had been in the shrine’s possession was designated as a {{ill|Nagasaki Prefecture cultural property|ja|長崎県指定文化財一覧|qid=Q11652661|lt=Nagasaki Prefecture cultural property}}<ref>[http://www.pref.nagasaki.jp/bunkadb/bunkazai_details_nomap.php?id=260 “Tripitaka of Takuzudama Shrine”]{{dead link|date=January 2018}} Nagasaki Prefecture, Cultural Properties of Nagasaki Prefecture</ref>, but it was stolen in October 2012 along with the “Standing Bronze Buddha Tathāgata” from {{ill|Kaijin Shrine|ja|海神神社|ko|가이진 신사|simple|Kaijin Shrine|zh|海神神社|qid=Q11559099}} and the “Seated Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva” from {{ill|Kannon-ji Temple|ja|観音寺 (対馬市)|ko|간논지 (나가사키현 쓰시마시)|qid=Q11630602|lt=Kannon-ji}} (the {{ill|Tsushima Buddha statue theft incident|ja|対馬仏像盗難事件|ko|쓰시마 불상 도난 사건|qid=Q18337378}})<ref>[http://www.nagasaki-np.co.jp/kiji/20121010/02.shtml “Two additional cases of cultural property theft discovered”]{{dead link|date=January 2018}} {{ill|The Nagasaki Shimbun|ja|長崎新聞|ko|나가사키 신문|qid=Q11652567}}, October 10, 2012</ref>. In January 2013, a group of {{ill|Korean nation|fr|Kankokujin|ja|韓国人|ko|한국인 (동음이의)|zh|韓國人|zh_min_nan|Hân-kok-lâng|zh_yue|韓國人|qid=Q11271251}} who attempted to bring the items into South Korea to sell them were detained, and the two Buddhist statues were recovered; however, the perpetrators stated that the Tripitaka had been “discarded in the fields and mountains around the shrine”<ref>[https://www.nikkei.com/article/DGXNASDG3000V_Q3A130C1CR0000/ “Man detained in Tsushima Buddhist statue theft; South Korean police recover stolen items”] {{ill|The Nikkei|arz|مؤشر نيكى|br|Nihon Keizai Shimbun (Nikkei)|ca|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|cv|Нихон кэйдзай симбун|de|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|eo|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|es|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|eu|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|fa|روزنامه نیهون کیزای|fi|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|fr|Nihon keizai shinbun|hi|निक्केई|id|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|it|Nihon Keizai Shinbun|ja|日本経済新聞|ko|니혼케이자이 신문|ms|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|no|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|pl|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|pt|The Nikkei|ru|Нихон кэйдзай симбун|sv|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|tr|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|uk|Ніхон кейдзай сімбун|vi|Nihon Keizai Shimbun|zh|日本經濟新聞|qid=Q1077694}}, January 30, 2013</ref>.
